scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for the user to refuse to loan her brother her vacation money. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the user is a 21-year-old female in her third year of university, studying business. She's working to put herself through school and has been saving money from her paychecks for a big vacation after she graduates. The fund currently has $2800, and she plans to use it for a cruise, trip to Japan, or exploring Europe. She's been saving for a while, sometimes putting away as much as 15% of her income, which shows she's been disciplined about it.

Her brother is 30, living with their parents, and is back in school to improve his job situation. He's been living with them for 1.5 years. He's in a tough job and is trying to better himself by going back to school. He hasn't been on a vacation in many years and has been hinting that he needs one. The parents suggested that he could start saving now to afford a trip, but he approached the sister instead, asking to borrow her vacation money for a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He argued that since she won't need the money for another two years, he can pay her back in time.

The sister refused, citing her brother's poor money management skills. She points out that despite earning about the same as her, he's always broke because he doesn't contribute to groceries or rent, unlike her. She's uncomfortable with the idea of lending him the money, doubting his ability to repay her on time. She also feels that her brother is making unfair comparisons, blaming her for being spoiled by their parents, while she attributes her financial discipline to her father and her university classes.

Now, the question is whether it's morally acceptable for her to refuse the loan. To evaluate this, I need to consider several factors: the moral obligations between siblings, the responsibility to manage one's own finances, fairness, and the potential consequences of lending the money.

First, siblings often have a moral obligation to support each other, especially in times of need. However, this obligation isn't absolute and can be influenced by various factors, such as the ability to help without causing undue harm to oneself, the likelihood of the request being fulfilled responsibly, and the fairness of the request.

In this case, the brother is in a difficult financial situation, trying to better himself by going back to school. He's been living with the parents for a while, and it seems he's struggling financially. He's hinting that he needs a vacation, which could be a way to relieve stress or take a break from his studies and job. However, he's asking to borrow money from his sister, who has been saving meticulously for her own future plans.

The sister has valid concerns about her brother's ability to manage money. He's always broke despite not contributing to groceries or rent, which suggests poor financial habits. She's worried he won't be able to repay her in time, which could cause problems for her when she graduates and wants to use the money for her vacation.

Additionally, she feels that the comparison her brother is making is unfair. She's been responsible with her money, saving for her future, while he's been less so. She attributes her financial discipline to her father and her university education, not to being spoiled by her parents, which adds to her frustration.

On the other hand, the brother is in a tough spot, trying to improve his life by going back to school and working. He's been living with the parents, which might mean he's relying on them for financial support. The parents suggested he start saving for a trip, implying they believe he should take responsibility for his own finances. However, he's come to his sister instead, perhaps because he feels he can't save enough on his own or because he's hoping she'll be more generous.

The sister's refusal could be seen as a responsible decision, given her brother's history of poor money management. She's protecting her own financial future, which is a valid consideration. However, it could also be seen as not supporting her brother when he's in need, which might be a moral failing.

Another angle is the fairness of the request. The sister has been saving for her vacation for years, and it's a significant goal for her. The brother is asking to use that money for his own trip, which might not be as urgent or important in her eyes. He's been in a difficult financial situation for a while, but he's also been in school, which might mean he's had the opportunity to save if he managed his money better.

Moreover, the sister's parents have already been helping him financially, which might mean he's not in a position to ask for more help, especially from his sister. The parents suggested he start saving now, which implies they believe he should take responsibility for his own finances, rather than relying on others.

In terms of consequences, if the sister lends her brother the money and he doesn't repay her, it could strain their relationship and leave her without the funds she's been saving for. On the other hand, refusing might lead to tension and resentment, especially if the brother feels she's not supporting him when he's in need.

Considering all these factors, it seems that the sister's decision to refuse the loan is morally acceptable. She's protecting her own financial future, which is a responsible decision, especially given her brother's history of poor money management. While it's important to support family members, it's also crucial to set boundaries to avoid enabling bad habits or causing harm to oneself.

Additionally, the sister has valid points about the unfairness of the comparison and the responsibility she's taken with her finances. She's not being spoiled; she's working hard and saving diligently. Her brother's frustration might stem from his own financial struggles and the pressure to improve his situation, but that doesn't necessarily make her obligation to help him any stronger.

In conclusion, while it's a tough situation, the sister's refusal to lend her brother her vacation money appears to be morally acceptable. She's prioritizing her own financial security and future goals, which is a responsible choice, especially given her brother's demonstrated inability to manage his finances effectively.
